Important information 
This climate-related disclosure contains climate-related and other forward-looking statements and  
metrics which are not, and should not be considered to be, guarantees, predictions or forecasts of  
future climate-related outcomes, financial performance or share prices. Those statements are subject 
to known and unknown risks, uncertainties and other factors, many of which are beyond the IAG New 
Zealand’s control. Readers are therefore cautioned not to place reliance on such statements in light of  
the uncertainty in climate metrics and modelling that limits the extent to which they are useful for 
decision-making. IAG New Zealand reserves the right to change its views in the future.
Please read the Important Notices in Appendix C of this climate-related disclosure and other guidance  
and limitations stated elsewhere in this climate-related disclosure to aid your understanding.
Figures and commentary relate to the financial year ended 30 June 2024, unless otherwise indicated.

Reporting group 
This climate-related disclosure is for IAG New Zealand Limited (a licensed insurer in 
New Zealand) and its subsidiaries. IAG New Zealand is the largest general insurer in the 
country, trading under the AMI, State, NZI, NAC, Lumley and Lantern brands, as well as 
providing the general insurance products distributed by ASB, BNZ, Westpac and The 
Co-operative Bank. 
IAG New Zealand is a wholly-owned subsidiary of IAG (NZ) Holdings Limited. First 
Rescue New Zealand Limited, IAG NZ Repairhub Limited, and Homehub Limited (the 
Hub Services), are also subsidiaries of IAG (NZ) Holdings Limited. The Hub Services 
are not insurers and are not included in IAG New Zealand’s reporting group for this 
climate-related disclosure. 
Insurance Australia Group Limited (referred to in this document as IAG Group) is the 
ultimate parent company of IAG New Zealand and IAG (NZ) Holdings Limited. Its shares 
are quoted on the Australian Stock Exchange and it also has debt securities listed on 
the NZDX Market operated by NZX Limited. IAG Group has released a voluntary climate-
related disclosure for FY24 (IAG Group climate-related disclosure), which can be found 
within IAG Group’s FY24 Annual Report on the IAG Group website. 
As First Rescue New Zealand Limited, IAG NZ Repairhub Limited and Homehub Limited 
are subsidiaries of IAG Group, the IAG Group climate-related disclosure and associated 
ESG Data Summary includes GHG emissions data for these companies.

IAG New Zealand acknowledges Tāngata Whenua in Aotearoa New Zealand and 
recognises their customary authority on the lands where our people and buildings  
are located.

Section 1: Governance | Kāwanatanga
Board oversight
IAG New Zealand’s Board of Directors (the Board) 
has oversight of the management of risks and 
opportunities for the organisation, including 
those related to climate change and our strategic 
response to address these. 
During FY24, the Board considered IAG New Zealand’s 
climate-related scenarios and the risks and opportunities 
that had been prioritised based on materiality, and 
discussed how our strategy may need to adapt to respond 
to these risks and opportunities.
The Board is supported by three Board committees: the 
Board Risk Committee, the Board Audit Committee and 
the Board People & Remuneration Committee. Together 
the Board and its standing committees are responsible for 
overseeing our climate-related risks and opportunities, 
our strategic response to them and the frameworks that 
support this work. The Board is also supported by IAG 
Group governance bodies relating to climate change and 
more information about this can be found in the climate-
related disclosure section of IAG Group’s FY24 Annual 
Report on the IAG Group website. 
The Board Risk Committee oversees the identification, 
assessment and mitigation of risks across IAG New Zealand, 
including climate-related risks. The Board Risk Committee 
is informed about these matters through updates provided 
by the Chief Risk Officer, which includes input to quarterly 
meetings of the Committee. 
The Board Audit Committee is responsible for reviewing 
our climate-related disclosure for adherence to legislation 
and the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards and 
recommending approval of the disclosure to the Board.  
The Committee’s role includes consideration of references 
to this climate-related disclosure in our financial 
statements. The Board Audit Committee receives updates 
from management throughout the year. 
The Board People & Remuneration Committee has 
responsibility for oversight of our Balanced Scorecard1, 
including the remuneration-related emissions metric 
discussed in Section 4. 
IAG New Zealand’s Board Skills Matrix, which is used to 
evaluate the composition and suitability of the Board’s 
skills, competencies and experience, includes an 
evaluation of the Board’s understanding and identification 
of climate-related risks and opportunities. During FY24 
three new non-executive directors were appointed to 
the Board, and we consider these appointments have 
enhanced the Board’s capability and experience related to 
climate-related risks and opportunities. 
The Board has visibility of our climate targets and 
progress against them as part of their review and approval 
of this climate-related disclosure, and associated Board 
update papers. In FY24 the IAG New Zealand Board 
approved this climate-related disclosure, and the metrics 
and targets disclosed.
1	 The Balanced Scorecard is a weighted performance framework used to assess Short Term Incentive remuneration and is balanced across a range of financial and  
non-financial measures designed to focus Executives on delivering IAG Group’s strategic and divisional objectives.
Introduction
IAG New Zealand’s core business and value chain 
are exposed to the impacts of climate change – 
both physical impacts (through weather events 
and resulting claims) and transition impacts 
(as Aotearoa New Zealand works towards 
decarbonisation). Our exposure to climate-
related risks requires us to have a strong focus 
on the sustainability of our business so that we 
can continue to meet the needs of our customers 
and shareholders. Claims arising out of weather 
events can be substantial and can adversely 
affect our financial and operational performance, 
therefore climate-related risks are closely 
managed.

Section 2: Strategy | Rautaki
Introduction to IAG New Zealand’s 
business model and strategy
IAG New Zealand is Aotearoa New Zealand’s 
largest general insurer, providing a range of 
retail and commercial insurance products to 
individuals, households and businesses. 
These products include vehicle, property, contents, business 
interruption, and liability. The products are sold directly 
by IAG New Zealand brands and also via intermediaries 
including insurance brokers and bank partners.
We are undertaking a two-phase business transformation. 
Phase one is focused on building the foundations for 
growth. It includes replacing legacy core systems, 
simplifying business processes, seeking to improve the 
customer experience and creating efficiencies in our 
business. The second phase is focused on growth through 
improved brand propositions including new products  
and services. 
The impacts of climate change are expected to be felt 
across different parts of the IAG New Zealand business 
model, whether that be how our products and services 
evolve to meet the changing needs and preferences of 
customers to insure and protect their assets, how we 
manage our supply chain to become more sustainable, the 
reinsurance terms available to us or the investment choices 
we make. A summary of the IAG New Zealand business 
model is shown in Figure 2, noting that some of these 
activities are carried out at an IAG Group level.

Climate scenario analysis – our 
approach and a summary of three 
entity level scenarios
Our approach
In FY24, IAG New Zealand conducted scenario analysis 
through the Climate Working Group, the NZLT and the 
Board with support from consultants WSP New Zealand. 
This involved updating outputs from a similar exercise 
undertaken in FY23. 
Our scenario analysis also leveraged the physical risk 
models underpinning our insurance and reinsurance risk 
assessments, with overlays applied to reflect the projected 
physical risk changes across a range of natural peril types. 
This analysis helps us investigate the sensitivity of our 
insurance portfolios to climate-related risk and highlights 
key trends in risk sensitivity.
IAG New Zealand was involved in creating the Insurance 
Council of New Zealand | Te Kāhui Inihua o Aotearoa 
insurance sector climate scenarios (ICNZ scenarios). Those 
scenarios have been used as a basis for the development 
of our own entity-level scenarios. During the development 
of our own scenarios, we reviewed and adjusted the ICNZ 
scenario short-term and medium-term time horizons as 
described below. 
•	 The short-term horizon of 2022-2025 was adjusted to 
2024-2027 to reflect our rolling three-year strategic 
planning and budget cycle outlook and was made in 
consideration of our Enterprise Risk Profile timeframe. 
This time horizon also aligns with our initial capital 
deployment to enhance risk modelling currently being 
conducted by the Natural Perils Uplift Project as detailed 
later in this climate-related disclosure. 
•	 The medium-term horizon of 2026-2035 was adjusted to 
2028-2035 to reflect the above change. 
•	 We adopted the long-term horizon in the ICNZ scenarios 
(2036-2050). 
Our climate scenario analysis was undertaken as part of 
IAG New Zealand’s wider strategy processes. 
Entity level climate scenarios
The IAG New Zealand entity level climate scenarios – Orderly, 
Disorderly and Hot House World – are outlined in Figure 3. 
These scenarios adopt the same underlying assumptions 
(except for time horizons) and data sets as the ICNZ’s Orderly, 
Disorderly, and Hot House World climate scenarios2 including 
the pathways used to construct the scenarios. A more 
detailed description of the underlying assumptions in respect 
of each entity level climate scenario is set out in Appendix B.
2	 Analysis conducted during the development of the ICNZ scenarios determined that energy pathways, carbon sequestration from afforestation; and negative emissions 
technology do not have a material impact on the insurance sector. However, the analysis acknowledges that there could be macroeconomic impacts.

Current impacts of climate change  
on our business
The impacts of climate change are expected to affect 
IAG New Zealand in two ways – directly and through our 
customers. It is the customer impact which is expected to be 
more material to us and have flow on effects to our business 
and our strategy. The changes we are expecting to see from 
the risks identified above are starting to occur, with some 
tangible – but not material – examples identified below. 
Current transition impacts
Our focus on reducing climate change risk and 
operational GHG emissions has included a shift to 
procurement of renewable electricity for our business,  
as well as ongoing conversion of our corporate motor 
vehicle fleet to hybrid vehicles. 
There has also been an increase in compliance costs, 
primarily due to the need for increased resourcing, to meet 
the mandatory climate-related disclosure requirements 
as well as managing consequential changes to our 
governance, risk and strategy processes.
In line with the rest of the market, our motor vehicle 
insurance portfolios are seeing increased demand for low 
emissions vehicle insurance.8
Current physical impacts
During FY24 IAG New Zealand customers made claims 
arising from 199 major weather-related events across 
the country compared to 28 events of that nature in the 
previous 12 months. Claim volumes from these 19 events 
were well below the previous 12 months due to the high 
volume of claims in FY23 resulting from the North Island 
floods and Cyclone Gabrielle.
Current and anticipated financial impacts 
of climate change on our business
We have chosen to apply the Adoption Provisions 1 and 2 
under NZ CS 2 in relation to disclosure of the current and 
anticipated financial impacts of climate-related impacts, 
risks and opportunities. This will allow us more time to 
develop and refine the methodology for reporting on  
these aspects.
Capital deployment and funding
Management of climate-related risks and opportunities 
forms part of our decision-making processes for capital 
deployment and funding including through internal 
budgeting processes and pricing/underwriting of our 
insurance products. These decision-making processes 
include:
•	 our capital and reinsurance strategy;
•	 the setting of our natural perils allowances and 
allocation of natural perils allowances, and;
•	 assessment of reinsurance costs.
We are investing in data uplift to improve our management 
of climate-related and other peril risk across our insurance 
portfolio. The aims of the Natural Perils Uplift Project 
include improved natural peril risk modelling to enable 
a greater understanding of climate-related risk. In FY24, 
we updated our flooding and coastal inundation hazard 
mapping, incorporating lessons from recent weather 
events in our other peril models and addressing known 
modelling limitations. 
Developing the transition planning 
aspects of our strategy
During FY24, the Board and NZLT reviewed the scenario 
analysis and prioritised risks and opportunities to begin to 
identify how our strategy may evolve and adapt. We have 
chosen to apply Adoption Provision 3 under NZ CS 2 in 
relation to the transition plan aspects of our strategy with 
further development planned in FY25.

Section 3: Risk Management | Te Whakahaerenga Tūraru
Risk Management Programme
Our Risk Management Programme is reviewed annually and 
encompasses frameworks, policies, standards, systems and 
processes to meet our prudential obligations as a licensed 
insurer under the Insurance Prudential Supervision Act 2010 
(IPSA) and, as a member of the IAG Group, APRA Prudential 
Standard CPS 220 (Risk Management). We have designed 
the Risk Management Programme to inform IAG New 
Zealand’s people on how to manage risk and to assist us to 
deliver on our strategy while meeting applicable regulatory 
and compliance obligations. 
Identification of risks
We identify risks facing our business, including climate-
related risks, using a combination of top-down and 
bottom-up approaches. Our Enterprise Risk Profile (ERP) 
identifies key strategic and emerging risks facing our 
business. The ERP undergoes ongoing monitoring with 
an annual review involving the NZLT and the Board. 
Prioritisation of climate-related risks compared to other 
types of risk occurs as part of these processes.
Climate-related risk has been part of the ERP since 
2014, evolving to capture the impacts of both physical 
and transition risks on our business. Our ERP currently 
includes two specific climate change risks, one relating 
to natural perils and one relating to our transition 
response, alongside other climate-related risks relating 
to reinsurance, affordability of insurance and potential 
government intervention. Emerging risks arising from 
climate-related stress testing and scenario analysis will 
also inform the ERP.
Assessment of risks
The Risk Management Programme employs a risk profiling 
methodology to enable an understanding of the key risks 
that could impact our ability to achieve our strategy. 
Developed through the Risk Assessment process, a Risk 
Profile captures information about each business unit’s 
objectives, risks associated with conducting that business 
and when relevant, the actions that are required to bring 
the level of risk to an acceptable position. 
Risks are given an inherent and residual assessment in 
accordance with our internally developed Risk Impact 
Matrix and Risk Heat Map. Tools used as part of this 
impact assessment include capital modelling, reinsurance 
catastrophe modelling, actuarial loss reserving and 
technical pricing models. When a risk is identified and 
assessed as having a greater impact and/or more likely to 
occur, it is considered key to the business and prioritised. 
Key controls must then be identified or implemented to 
manage the risk. 
Through the scenario analysis process and using the 
same time horizons as applied to the scenarios described 
in Section 2 above, we have evaluated the inherent 
likelihood and severity of climate-related risks, assigning 
materiality ratings for each priority climate-related risk 
with reference to our Risk Impact Matrix. Our Risk Impact 
Matrix considers the likelihood of each risk materialising 
over the next ten years.
Management of risks
Our Risk Appetite Statement (RAS) governs the 
management of risks, including climate-related risks, at 
an enterprise and business unit level. The RAS is reviewed 
and updated annually and outlines the level of risk that 
we are willing to accept in pursuit of our objectives10. The 
focus of the RAS is to confirm that in taking on risk, the 
business can continue to be resilient, deliver its business 
plan, adhere to legal and regulatory obligations, and meet 
the expectations of stakeholders. The management of the 
ERP and business unit Risk Profiles is monitored to ensure 
ongoing adherence to the RAS parameters.
The management and monitoring of climate-related risks 
follow our Risk Management Programme, which is also 
subject to annual review, and aligns with our three lines  
of accountability operating model11.

also being considered, but not deemed material or relevant to the scope of this climate-related disclosure for IAG New Zealand.

managing the risk and advises as needed; Line 3 – Internal Audit who provides independent assurance over Line 1 and Line 2 control effectiveness.

Appendix A: Glossary
Table A1: Glossary
Term
Definition
Adaptation 
Practical actions taken to manage risks arising from climate change to enhance resilience and minimise damage. 
Aotearoa New Zealand  
Climate Standards
Standards issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB) that comprise the climate-related disclosure framework.
Board (the Board)
The Board of Directors of IAG New Zealand Limited.
Carbon dioxide equivalent 
(CO2e)
The universal unit of measurement to indicate the global warming potential of each of the seven GHGs, expressed in terms of the global warming potential of one unit of 
carbon dioxide for 100 years.  It is used to evaluate releasing (or avoiding releasing) any GHGs against a common basis.
Climate-related risk 
The potential negative impacts of climate change on an entity. See also the definitions of physical risks and transition risks.
Climate-related opportunities
The potentially positive climate-related outcomes for an entity. Efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change can produce opportunities for entities, such as through 
resource efficiency and cost savings, the adoption and utilisation of low-emissions energy sources, the development of new products and services, and building resilience 
along the value chain.
Decarbonisation 
The process of reducing carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions through the implementation of initiatives such as energy efficiency, fleet transition, and using low- carbon or 
renewable power sources. 
Emissions
The release of GHGs into the atmosphere.
Financial impacts
The translation of impacts into current or anticipated impacts on financial performance, financial position and cash flows.
FTE
Full-time equivalent (employee).
Greenhouse Gases (GHGs) 
Gases in Earth's atmosphere that trap heat. They include carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and fluorinated gases.
GHG Protocol
GHG Protocol supplies a widely used greenhouse gas accounting standard.
Global warming potential
A factor describing the radiative forcing impact (degree of harm to the atmosphere) of one unit of a given GHG relative to one unit of carbon dioxide (CO2).
Goal
A broad, overarching goal which acts as our guiding principle for action, setting the direction of our interim targets.
Impacts
The effects (also referred to as consequences or outcomes) of climate change occurring for an entity. These effects will, in turn, depend on the impacts of climate change 
on the broader socioeconomic and ecological systems an entity operates within (including an entity’s value chain).
Metric
A quantity indicative of the level of historical, current, and forward-looking climate-related risks and opportunities for a given entity. These indicators are used to track 
climate-related risks and opportunities and can also be used to measure progress against targets over the duration of the period for which a target is set.
Net zero insurer
Achieving net zero emissions across all operations, while actively enhancing climate resilience and capturing opportunities through the transition.
Physical risks
Risks related to the physical impacts of climate change. Physical risks emanating from climate change can be event-driven (acute) such as increased severity of extreme 
weather events. They can also relate to longer-term shifts (chronic) in precipitation and temperature and increased variability in weather patterns, such as sea level rise.

Appendix B: Methodologies and Assumptions
Section 2 – Strategy
Please refer to the description of each scenario in Section 
2 of this climate-related disclosure. Additional underlying 
assumptions are set out below.
Scenarios: Underlying assumptions
Orderly: Net Zero 2050 
•	 By 2050, transport, energy and industry sectors are largely 
decarbonised.
•	 Strong development in data and technologies over the short- 
and medium-term, including collaboration and government 
investment.
Disorderly: Delayed Transition
•	 By 2050, there is some way to go for energy sector 
decarbonisation, including for buildings.
•	 Beginning in the early 2030s, a significant hinge point occurs 
where decarbonisation of transport, energy and industry moves 
at pace. 
•	 Delayed investments in sustainable development in the short-
term. More rapid, disruptive uptake of sustainable technology 
occurs in the long-term. 
Hot House World: Current Policies 
•	 Economic growth is high, combined with material-intensive 
production and consumption patterns and a strong reliance on 
abundant fossil fuel resources.
•	 Lagging data and technology uptake compared to other OECD 
countries. Adaptation technology, such as data and digital 
solutions to support adaptation starts to take off in the long-
term. There is limited mitigation technology available. 
Risk and opportunity identification: 
Assumptions and limitations
When identifying and assessing climate-related risks and 
opportunities, assumptions were made regarding the financial 
impacts of identified risks and opportunities to determine 
materiality and prioritisation. These assumptions were based 
on information in the ICNZ scenarios and IAG New Zealand 
scenarios, internal business knowledge and external insights.
Physical risk modelling: Limitations
The physical risk modelling approach is limited by the lack of 
region-specific, high-quality scientific literature addressing 
future-climate severe weather events (weather that happens in 
a wholly different state of the climate) in Aotearoa New Zealand. 
To address this challenge, we have invested in improving our 
understanding of the impact of a changing climate on severe 
weather and physical risks.
The potential for a step-change in coastal hazards (driven by 
sea level rise approaching the threshold levels around which 
our coastal communities have been designed) is not currently 
addressed by our physical risk modelling. We have invested in 
work to better quantify coastal inundation risk in current and 
future climates.
Other complex or less likely future-climate severe weather trends 
not captured by our modelling approach include:
•	 Changes to the impacts from ex-tropical cyclones, which are 
poorly represented in historical datasets. 
•	 Changes to the physical size, longevity and intensity of severe 
convective storms.
•	 Emergence of wildfire risk in Aotearoa New Zealand, which is 
not strongly represented in historical claims. 
•	 Potential non-linear responses to compounding wind and  
rain damage. 
•	 Increased liquefaction risk driven by rising groundwater levels 
impacted by sea level rise in coastal areas. 
•	 Increased tsunami risk driven by rising sea levels.
These factors would generally act to increase climate-related 
risks above and beyond the modelled scenarios.
source: FY24 IAG New Zealand Climate-related Disclosure.pdf

Additional metric categories: Definitions, 
methodology, assumptions and limitations
Percentage of IAG New Zealand insured homes currently at 
high risk of flood: For the purposes of this metric, ‘high risk’ 
is defined as insured homes that we expect to incur at least 
a doubling of the premiums payable by the insured by fully 
charging policyholders for expected flood costs (if we started 
fully charging for those expected costs today). This is based on 
an estimate of IAG New Zealand insured homes, updated FY24 
modelling of riverine flood risk as at 31 May 2024, with only 
high-confidence modelling included, and as such is different to 
previous projections made by IAG New Zealand.
Flood risk assessments combine the estimated likelihood and 
depth of flooding across the full spectrum of possible events, 
incorporating IAG New Zealand’s understanding of building 
vulnerability and insurance response, and customer policy terms 
such as sum insured and excess.
Our flood model relies upon council flood studies and a vendor 
model for flood hazard incidence when a council study is 
unavailable. 
Flood modelling is uncertain in Aotearoa New Zealand as there is 
regional variation in the quality and availability of elevation data 
and local flood studies. 
This metric incorporates riverine flood risk only. We are working 
towards national risk modelling of coastal inundation and we will 
consider incorporating coastal risk in this metric as the modelling 
matures. We anticipate this metric would be higher in future time 
horizons and especially in the Hot House World scenario.
Total vehicles per capita in New Zealand in 2024: For the 
purposes of this metric, data has been sourced from Deloitte 
Access Economics, and calculated from New Zealand Ministry of 
Transport Fleet statistics and Statistics NZ National Population 
Estimates for June 2024. 
An ARIMAX regression model was applied to historical 
data series and identified key explanatory variables (real 
consumption growth per working age person) and change in 
the unemployment rate level. Existing Deloitte macroeconomic 
forecasts for those variables were then used to derive vehicles 
per working age population forecast baseline, and then adjusted 
to vehicles per capita. These forecasts have been completed at 
the total fleet level, and do not consider how different categories 
of the fleet are impacted by mode shift (e.g. buses, trucks). 
Appendix B
Deloitte completed some scenario forecasts to adjust the 
baseline forecast to account for potential mode shift. Deloitte 
assume lower mode shift than the Climate Change Commission, 
due in part to the significant infrastructure development and 
subsequent behavioural changes which would be required, 
and that a number of policy initiatives assumed by the Climate 
Change Commission have since not gone ahead. 
Percentage of electric vehicles in New Zealand’s current 
overall vehicle fleet: For the purposes of this metric, data 
has been sourced from Ministry of Transport fleet statistics to 
determine the current EV market penetration for all vehicle 
types. The result above is for battery electric vehicles only and 
excludes plug in hybrids and hybrids. 
This result is for the overall vehicle fleet as at June 2024 and is 
slightly higher if only light vehicles are considered (2.0%), or when 
looking at certain, more populous regions e.g., Auckland (2.9% 
light vehicle share). 
The opportunity can be measured by the difference in EV 
portfolio performance against existing motor vehicle portfolios. 
Despite the current low market penetration, the Climate Change 
Commission predicts growth in EVs to 2035 which is reflected in 
our scenario analysis. 
Capital deployment metric: For the purposes of this metric, 
this captures specific areas of operational expenditure relating 
to work undertaken relating to IAG New Zealand (including IAG 
Group spend on New Zealand perils work) relating to climate 
change. The following table details the included initiatives along 
with relevant assumptions and limitations.
Initiative
Commentary
Natural perils uplift (IAG New Zealand)
Spend on the Natural Perils Uplift project from within IAG New Zealand. Relates to spend on 
flood model uplift and implementation into pricing. 
Natural perils uplift (Group)
Spend on the New Zealand Natural Perils Uplift project from within the Group Natural Perils 
team. Includes purchasing of datasets and consultancy spend.
Sustainability Upgrades
Spend on sustainability upgrade aspects of claims relating to total loss of a home, via 
applicable policies (e.g. solar water heating). This number relates to claims closed during 
FY24. This is based on payment data from the ‘Sustainability Upgrade’ coverage in our claims 
system. No significant further payments were found, including through manual inspection of 
claims with notes mentioning ‘sustainability’.
Customer climate change education 
– social media customer engagement 
(e.g., Wild Weather Tracker, Disaster 
Claims Hub)
Spend on social media posts and marketing leverage related to climate-related content, 
specifically the Wild Weather Tracker, Emergency Checklist, preparedness advice (wildfires), 
emissions reduction and EVs. Only external spend in relation to customer education 
campaigns is included (internal resource for this activity not included).
NZI EV Guide campaign costs
Spend on development of collateral and promotion of the NZI EV Fleet Guide during FY24. 
System changes
Portion of spend related to updating business system platforms to enable our business 
to respond to climate-related risks. Percentage spend is based on proportion of project 
deliverables estimated as being related to responding to physical and transition risks relating 
to climate change.
Climate Disclosure Project
Spend on project to respond to the XRB Climate Disclosure requirements.

Costs incurred responding to the New Zealand Government’s Land Classification Framework 
in response to changes in flood risk as a result of climate change.
